By Region (FY’25 & FY’30F)

The North region leads India’s confectionery market with a share rising from 33.0% in FY’25 to 33.6% in FY’30F at a
CAGR of 6.6%, driven largely by Delhi NCR region. The region’s high-income urban base and strong retail infrastructure
for modern trade and online trade network support demand, particularly during festive peaks like Diwali which leads to tap
the market smoothly. Lucknow and Kanpur contribute through dense general trade networks and sweet consumption habits,
increasingly tapped by organized players.

The South region, steady at 24.5%–24.6% at a CAGR of 6.3% from the FY'25 to FY'30F respectively, sees growth from
Bengaluru (~7.8%), Hyderabad (~6.5%), and Chennai (~6.0%). Bengaluru’s young demographic and high retail adoption
drive impulse and premium sales. Hyderabad’s rising incomes and gifting culture, and Chennai’s preference for milk-based
sweets, sustain steady demand through both general and modern trade.

In the West, with share from 20.0% in FY'25 to 20.2% in FY'30F at a CAGR of 6.4%, sees the growth in the cities like
Mumbai (~9.2%), Ahmedabad (~5.5%), Pune (~5.0%), and Surat (~4.0%) are key markets. Mumbai leads on account of
premium retail and affluent demand, while Pune’s young population favours new-age confectionery. Ahmedabad and Surat
contribute strong festive-driven volumes through deep-rooted kirana networks and regional sweet preferences.

India’s Economy Confectionery Market Size, FY’19-FY’25-FY’30F

The India’s economy confectionery market includes confectionery product SKUs priced at INR 1–10. In FY’25, economy-
priced confectionery market is valued at INR 50.5 thousand crores, reflecting their continued relevance among price-
sensitive consumers, particularly in Tier 2–3 cities and rural areas. The growth in the segment is driven by low unit pricing
(INR1–5) and widespread availability through kirana stores and distributor-led networks.

In 2023, Nestlé India’s Munch, which continued to strengthen its position in the affordable chocolate segment by providing
chocolate at INR 5, Munch rolled out multiple youth engagement campaigns, including IPL team partnerships with Punjab

and augmented reality experiences targeted at younger consumers. In 2024, Nestlé launched the “Utha MUNCH, Dikha

strong retail presence. (Source: MediaNews4U)

Looking ahead, growth in the economy confectionery segment is projected to moderate. This reflects a gradual shift in
consumer preferences toward premium and differentiated confectionery formats. While economy products are likely to
retain their volume advantage, their value contribution is expected to stabilize over the time.

Genesis and Innovation; Future Guidance, Growth Drivers

Historic Evolution: India’s confectionery market transitioned from traditional mithai to organized, packaged sweets during
the 1990s–2000s, driven by urbanization, rising incomes, and retail modernization. Brands like Cadbury, Nestlé, Perfetti,
Parle, and Haldiram’s led this shift by introducing hygienic, mass-priced (INR 1–INR 5) chocolates and candies, expanding
reach across rural India. By 2010, packaged confectionery accounted a major proportion of total urban share. Product
innovation during this phase focused on shelf-stable milk chocolates, hard-boiled candies, and toffees, while packaging
modernization and small-unit pricing helped expand rural access and impulse buying behavior.

Present Landscape: The market today balances affordable indulgence and premium demand. Economy-priced products
dominate rural sales, while urban markets favor premium and hybrid categories such as wafer chocolates and milk sweets.
Impulse snacking, hygienic packaging, and digital-first campaigns through Q-commerce and D2C channels are redefining
consumption. Companies like Mars Wrigley and Nestlé India have shifted towards 50:50 TV–digital media spend ratios as
per data published by Economic Times in April 2025, while Parle and ITC are focusing on value packs and regional flavour.

Future Outlook: The sector is increasingly driven by product and format innovation, with manufacturers blending
indulgence with functionality through fortified chocolates, healthier formulations, and novel textures and flavors.
Innovation in packaging, portioning, and personalization is improving speed-to-market and enabling rapid portfolio
refreshes. Manufacturers are also experimenting with new chocolate formats such as filled bars, layered chocolates,
bite-sized minis, spreads, and wafer-based chocolate products to diversify consumption occasions and appeal to
younger consumers seeking variety and convenience. Urban millennials and Gen Z are expected to favor clean-label,
premium, and plant-based confectionery, while innovations in processing and shelf-life extension are supporting the
expansion of gifting-oriented and milk-based confectionery beyond festive demand cycles.

Overview of Major Domestic and International Brands in India’s Economy Confectionery Market

The India’s economy confectionery market segment of product SKUs (INR 1–10) reflects a distinct divide between
international and domestic brand dominance. While international players such as Mondelez International Inc., Mars
International Pvt. Ltd., Nestle India Ltd. and Perfetti Van Melle Group have maintained a foothold through legacy brands
like Éclairs, Perk, Munch, Snickers, Alpenliebe, and Mentos, their presence is limited to a few SKUs in this low-price
segment.

In contrast, domestic brands, including Shellz India Limited, DS Group, Kayempee Foods, and Parle Products, demonstrate
deeper penetration with a broader and more diversified portfolio tailored for value-conscious consumers. This indicates a
strategic alignment by domestic firms towards keeping high-volume and low-unit price SKUs that resonate with mass-
market demand, especially in rural and semi-urban region.

Drivers & Market Opportunities

Rising Disposable Incomes And Retail Penetration Driving Market For Confectionery Products

India’s per capita Gross National Disposable Income (GNDI) has increased consistently from INR 1.45 lakh in FY19 to an
estimated INR 2.33 lakh in FY25\. Income growth accelerated in the post-FY21 period, peaking at 17.8% in FY22 and
stabilizing during FY24–FY25. This sustained expansion in disposable incomes is strengthening consumers’ spending
capacity on discretionary categories such as confectionery. Improved income visibility, alongside deeper penetration of
modern trade, e-commerce, and neighborhood retail, is driving higher consumption frequency and premiumization.
Consequently, confectionery demand is increasingly evolving from occasion-led purchases to everyday consumption.

Favorable Demographics & Youth Population Encouraging Confectionery Consumption

India’s demography is characterized by a significant child, adolescents, and young adults’ population that provides a strong
and recurring demand for confectionery products. Children and early adolescents drive high-volume consumption through
frequent, low-priced impulse purchases, while Gen Z consumers increasingly influence demand for new formats, flavors,
and experiential offerings such as gummies and novelty confectionery. The emerging Gen Alpha (individuals born after
2010) is further accelerating confectionery consumption. Among young adults, confectionery is gaining relevance as an
affordable indulgence and on-the-go snack. Collectively, this customer segment contributes to both current and future sales
for confectionery products.

increased digital adoption (UPI, Aadhaar-linked payments), and entrepreneurial activity-especially post-COVID migration
reversals played a role in encouraging new store openings in both rural and semi-urban regions.

Private Label Growth

Modern trade refers to organized retail formats such as supermarkets, hypermarkets, and retail chains that follow structured
operations, rely on centralized procurement, and are run by professionally managed systems. In modern trade sectors the
products provided by private label brands are priced 25–40% lower than branded items, making them appealing to price-
sensitive consumers. Private label manufactures such as Parsons Nutritional, Helenz Lifesciences, Dhiman Foods Pvt. Ltd,
Candico India Ltd. have expanded their private label offerings, including Baked Confectionery, Chocolate & Milky
Confectionery, and Sugar Confectionery, using efficient supply chains to maintain affordability and quality. Agreements
with manufacturers focus on exclusive supply contracts, ensuring steady product flow at competitive prices.

The expansion of private label portfolios in modern trade is also driving higher confectionery sales volumes,
particularly in impulse and value-driven categories. Retailers increasingly promote private label confectionery through in-
store visibility, bundled offers, and shelf prioritization, encouraging trial and repeat purchases. The lower price points
enable consumers to purchase larger pack sizes or buy multiple variants, thereby increasing basket size and category
penetration. Additionally, modern retailers leverage data-driven assortment planning and consumer insights to
introduce new flavors, healthier alternatives, and seasonal variants under private labels. As a result, confectionery products
under private labels are witnessing higher turnover and faster shelf rotation, contributing to the overall growth of
confectionery sales within modern trade channels.

Market Opportunities

Growth of E-Commerce in General with Focus on Gifting and Festive SKUs

India’s e-commerce sector has seen robust growth, expanding from INR 2.1 trillion in 2019 to a projected INR >6 trillion
by 2025, with festive seasons playing a major role. During these periods, Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) rose from INR
35.0 crores in 2019 to an estimated INR 117.4 crores in 2025. A key contributor to this surge is the rising popularity of
gifting and festive SKUs, particularly in categories like food and beverages, including confectionery. Products such as
chocolates, gourmet sweets, dry fruits, and curated hampers in exclusive festive packaging are in high demand during
occasions like Diwali, Eid, and Christmas. Notably, confectionery and bakery items accounted for 2-3% of Diwali spending
in India in 2025, reflecting their growing importance in festive gifting.

Fusion of Traditional and Modern Flavors and Innovative Packaging needs

Amid a rapidly modernizing FMCG landscape, the Indian confectionery sector is entering a phase of growth driven by
product and flavour innovation. The growing elderly consumer base is increasingly preferring new-age indulgent
products that combine traditional Indian flavours with modern confectionery formats. For instance, Haldiram’s
Nagpur launched its Cocobay chocolate range with fruit and spice flavours such as Chili Guava and Cranberry, highlighting
how brands are innovating on flavours to suit local tastes.

In addition to flavour experimentation, innovative packaging formats are playing a critical role in driving consumer
appeal and convenience. Manufacturers are introducing resealable pouches, portion-controlled packs, premium gift
boxes, and sustainable packaging materials to enhance product usability and shelf visibility. Attractive and ergonomic
packaging designs are helping brands position confectionery products as premium gifting options and on-the-go snacks,
particularly during festive seasons and social occasions. Furthermore, modern packaging technologies are being used to
improve product freshness, extend shelf life, and enable better branding through vibrant graphics and transparent
windows, thereby strengthening consumer engagement and purchase intent across both modern trade and e-commerce
channels.

Trends & Development

Rise of Affordable Indulgence, Snackification, Fusion of Traditional and Modern Flavors

The Indian confectionery market has seen a significant transformation, driven by the shift in tastes of urban and semi-urban
consumers. With rising disposable incomes and a growing aspiration for lifestyle pattern with global trends, affordable
indulgence has emerged as a key consumption driver. Small-pack, low-cost options priced under INR 10 have penetrated
Tier 2/3 cities, making innovative flavors and textures more accessible.

Snackification is transforming Indian confectionery, with brands incorporate traditional flavors like paan, gulkand, raw
mango, and jaggery into modern formats such as candies, lollipops, and wafers. These hybrid products cater to on-the-go
lifestyles while recall nostalgia, creating a unique fusion that appeals to both traditional tastes and modern preferences.
From Pulse’s tangy twist, American Cow to Desi Popz and chocolate-coated wafers, these innovations reflect a fusion and
growing trend in confectionery market.

    Figure 7-1: Traditional and Modern Flavors Snackification Products Among Indian Confectionery Brands

Growing Preference for Product Innovations

Product innovation in the Indian confectionery market is driven by adjustments in format, texture, flavour composition,
and price architecture, particularly in the mass and economy segments. Innovations such as development of multi-texture
products, where a single confectionery item combines different physical characteristics such as hard, soft, liquid, or creamy
components is altering the consumption experience. Further, the use of Indian flavour profiles - Tangy, sour, spicy, or
floral flavours are being incorporated into product offerings. Innovation is also occurring through non-traditional
chocolate formats, which extend chocolate consumption beyond conventional bars into more interactive or versatile forms.

Affordability is aspect in product innovation. New products are commonly designed below the ₹20 price point through
smaller unit sizes, high flavour intensity, and value-focused products, supporting frequent purchases. Additionally,
variety within a single product, such as multiple flavours or textures, is being used to increase engagement without
materially increasing cost.

Increase in Festival-Led Consumption

Festivals have been peak periods for confectionery sales in India, and this trend has only boost in recent years, with
consumers increasingly purchasing sweets and chocolates as preferred gifts during these celebrations.

    •    During Diwali 2025 festive period, a LocalCircles survey published in October 2025 found that 74% of urban
         households consumed traditional sweets at least three times a month, while 79% consumed sweet bakery or
         packaged products such as cakes, biscuits, chocolates, and candies with the same frequency. This represented an
         increase of over 40% in frequent sweet consumption compared to 2024.
    •    Similarly, festive spending during Rakhi 2025 surged further, with Confederation of All India Traders (CAIT)
         projecting retail trade of around INR 17,000 crore and an additional ~INR 4,000 crore from sweets, dry fruits, gift
         hampers and related categories highlighting the growing economic weight of Raksha Bandhan for confectionery
         and gifting players.
    •    During Christmas 2024, despite a 5–20% price hike in cakes and chocolates, retailers across major metros like
         Pune, Delhi, and Bengaluru reported a 25–50% surge in confectionery sales, driven by strong consumer demand
         for chocolate, gift boxes, and baked confectionery like plum cakes and cookies.

Innovation in Confectionery Segment

Innovation Trends

The Market is largely focused on volume, with limited innovation observed particularly at lower price products.

Total packaging retail volumes grew from 117.2 billion units in 2019 to 131.7 billion units in 2025E, indicating consistent
market expansion. However, this growth has largely been underpinned by the dominance of flexible packaging, which
reached 130.8 billion units in 2025E, up from 116.3 billion units in 2019. Within this, flexible plastic remained the
leading pack type, accounting for 114.0 billion units in 2025E, highlighting manufacturers' continued reliance on cost-
effective, scalable solutions to meet mass-market demand.


                                                                     173
Innovation in pack formats has remained largely incremental. The emergence of stand-up pouches, registering usage for
the first time in 2023 (0.1 million units), reflects early-stage experimentation but remains negligible in volume terms. Rigid
plastic has shown steady growth from 370 million units in 2019 to 410.0 million units in 2025E driven by applications in
count lines and boxed assortments; however, these formats cater mainly to mid-to-premium segments. Price sensitivity
continues to be a major barrier to broader adoption of innovative or sustainable packaging formats, especially in sugar
confectionery where 5 grams and below pack sizes are projected to account for 88% of volumes by 2028. This presents
an opportunity for players to develop differentiated, cost-effective solutions that align with evolving consumer preferences.

Technological Usage: Automation in Production

Driven by increasing consumer demand, rigid food safety standards, and the need for cost-efficient operations,
manufacturers are rapidly adopting automation and digital technologies across their production lines. While large players
such as Mondelez, Nestlé, and ITC have invested heavily in fully automated smart factories, small and medium enterprises
(SMEs) are also beginning to incorporate semi-automated systems. Adoption of technologies such as programmable logic
controllers (PLCs), robotic packing arms, AI-powered quality control systems, and IoT-based real-time monitoring is
becoming increasingly common.

The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for Food Processing, launched by the Government of India in 2021 with
an outlay of INR10,900 crore, has further accelerated technology adoption, particularly in automation and sustainability.
This includes financial support for machinery upgrades, smart packaging systems, and hygiene-focused contactless
production.

Market Challenges and Threats

Low Brand Loyalty in Value Segment for Confectionery Market

In confectionery market, low brand loyalty remains one of the most continuous challenges, especially for SME players.
The value segment is largely driven by impulse purchases, high price sensitivity, and low product differentiation factors
that make it difficult for brands to retain customers.

Consumers, particularly in rural and semi-urban areas, often view products like toffees, lollipops, and sugar candies as
interchangeable, and are quick to switch brands based on minor changes in price, taste, or availability. This behavior is
further escalated by the strong presence of local and unorganized players who can undercut prices and rapidly adapt to local
tastes. This environment creates a tough battlefield where even quality or consistency may not be enough to secure repeat
buyers. Building a loyal customer base becomes difficult without continuous visibility at the point of sale, innovative pricing
strategies (e.g., INR 1 – INR 2 SKUs), and localized brand-building efforts. In such a fragmented and price-driven



                                                                    175
landscape, low brand loyalty directly limits long-term brand value, market share stability, and investment returns for SMEs
trying to grow sustainably.

Margin Pressures Due to Input/Raw Material Cost Volatility

Companies in India's economical confectionery sector are struggling with significant margin pressures due to volatile raw
material costs. Key inputs such as sugar and edible oils have experienced notable price fluctuations. For instance, ex-mill
sugar prices in Maharashtra for the S-30 grade rose from INR 3,565 per quintal in mid-January 2025 to INR 3,790 per
quintal by mid-February 2025, marking a 6.5% increase in just one month. This surge is attributed to a 12% year-on-
year decline in sugar production, driven by adverse weather conditions and early mill closures.

Given that products in the economical segment are typically sold at fixed low-price points (INR 1–INR 10 SKUs),
manufacturers have limited flexibility to pass these increased costs onto consumers. Consequently, SMEs face the dilemma
of absorbing higher input costs, which erodes profit margins, or compromising on product quality, which can affect brand
reputation and customer retention. The lack of economies of scale and limited access to procurement strategies further
intensify these challenges for SMEs, making it vital to explore cost-effective sourcing of raw material and operational
efficiencies to sustain profitability in this volatile market landscape.

Competition from Local Unorganized Players

In the FY’25, organized sector holds 60.7% of the market, whereas the unorganized sector holds 39.3% of market share.
Despite the majority share of organized players, competition from the unorganized sector remains significant. Competition
from local unorganized players remains a significant challenge for companies across the board. These players comprising
regional manufacturers, cottage-scale producers, and local vendors, offer products at ultra-competitive price points, often
in the INR 1 to INR 5 range, appealing to price-sensitive consumers. Since, hard-boiled confectionery items do not require
high-tech setups, leading to increase of numerous unorganized small players across the country.

              Figure 0-33: Market Share by Company Type in Indian Confectionery Market for FY’25




                                    39.3%

The unorganized sector's dominance is particularly evident in rural and semi-urban areas, where they leverage minimal
overheads, flexible supply chains, and strong relationships with local retailers to ensure last-mile availability. This allows
them to undercut formal brands, making it challenging for organized players to maintain market share.

Moreover, the unorganized sector often operates with minimal compliance to food safety regulations, allowing them to
reduce costs further. The fragmented nature of the industry leads to inconsistencies in quality and standards, affecting both
domestic consumption and export potential.

Seasonal Demand Dependency

Seasonal demand dependency remains a structural challenge within India confectionery segment, interrupt consistent sales
cycles and complicating supply chain management. The market typically sees a spike in demand during the festive period

                                                                       176
(July to February), aligned with Raksha Bandhan, Diwali, Christmas, and the academic calendar. However, these high-
demand windows are offset by sharp declines during summer months and exam seasons, especially in rural markets where
school children constitute a primary consumer base. It is seen that confectionery manufacturers in Indore reported up to a
40% decline in sales during the off-season, with many SMEs reducing output and operating below installed capacity due
to diminished rural orders and school closures (Times of India).

Rise of Healthier Options

The rising consumer interest in healthier snacking driven by preferences for healthier alternatives, natural, and additive-
free products is gradually influencing among the consumer segment. However, this shift faces significant resistance within
the economical segment, where affordability, taste, and availability remain key drivers. About 58% of Indian consumers,
especially in rural and semi-urban areas, cite high prices as the primary barrier to adopting healthier options. Regulatory
mandates from the FSSAI, such as compulsory labelling of sugar and fat content, have further raised compliance costs
posing a challenge for manufacturers striving to keep products affordable.

Despite these hurdles, a niche but growing segment of medicated and functional confectionery is gaining traction, especially
in urban markets. Companies like Power Gummies, Kapiva, Man Matters, Gummy Vites, and Zingavita are offering
products such as Ashwagandha-infused gummies, Shilajit toffees, biotin and multivitamin gummies, and melatonin-
based sleep aids. While these products cater to health-conscious consumers seeking convenience and wellness, their reach
in price-sensitive and rural markets remains limited due to higher costs, weaker distribution networks, and competition
from unbranded local players. As a result, health-forward confectionery continues to struggle for mass adoption in India’s
economical segment.

Regulatory Hurdles for Export

India’s economical confectionery sector, which includes affordable and mass-market products like toffees, candies, and
lollipops, faces considerable regulatory challenges that hinder its export growth. Both large players and SMEs are affected
by a fragmented and often overlapping regulatory structure, inadequate food testing infrastructure, and the inability to
consistently meet stringent international safety and packaging standards.

Export consignments are frequently rejected due to non-compliance with food safety norms abroad; while evolving
domestic policies such as bans on recycled packaging or sudden export restrictions further increase uncertainty for
exporters. Moreover, infrastructure limitations and logistic & supply delays make it harder to compete globally, especially
for companies based in landlocked or rural areas. These systemic challenges not only impact product credibility in overseas
markets but also discourage long-term investments in export-focused growth strategies within the sector.

    •    India’s food export sector is burdened by fragmented regulatory oversight, with multiple agencies like FSSAI,
         APEDA, and BIS imposing overlapping requirements that create confusion and increase compliance costs for
         confectionery exporters.
    •    Sudden policy shifts, such as changes in export tariffs or product bans, make it difficult for exporters to plan and
         maintain buyer relationships.
    •    India’s inadequate food testing infrastructure, marked by outdated equipment and a shortage of skilled personnel,
         often results in inconsistent quality checks and frequent rejection of confectionery export consignments.
    •    Indian confectionery exports have faced over 500 food safety rejections in the EU since 2020 due to contamination
         and non-compliance.

Threats and Risk

The Indian confectionery market, include intense price competition, especially in the value segment, which is increased by
the presence of unbranded and local players offering similar products at lower costs. Additionally, shifting consumer
preferences towards healthier options, regulatory pressures for clearer labelling and ingredient disclosures, and supply chain
disruptions all present significant challenges. As consumer demand evolves, brands must navigate these risks while
maintaining product quality, affordability, and relevance in an increasingly competitive landscape.

                                                               Source: Ken Research Analysis

FSSAI Regulation on Sugar and Ingredients

The FSSAI has established comprehensive regulations governing the composition, use, and quality of sugars and
sweetening agents used in confectionery products in India, such as candies, toffees, sweets, and chewing gums, to ensure
food safety and consumer protection. These include strict purity and composition standards for various sugars commonly
used in confectionery manufacturing, including refined sugar, khandsari, cube, bura, and icing sugar.

Artificial sweeteners such as Aspartame, Sucralose, and Saccharin, used in sugar-free or reduced-sugar confectionery are
permitted only within specified purity limits (98.0%–99.9%) and are subject to controls on toxic residues. Traditional
sweeteners like jaggery, used in certain confectionery products, must meet prescribed moisture and sucrose content
requirements and be free from harmful additives.

In addition, food additives used in confectionery formulations must be FSSAI-approved, and the use of added colour is
generally prohibited in sweetening agents, ensuring compliance with safety and quality standards across confectionery
products in the Indian market.

                               0-10: FSSAI Regulation on Sugar and Ingredients Table




                                                                            179
                             Source: Food Safety and Standards (food product standards) regulations, 2020 & Ken Research Analysis


FSSAI Regulation on Labelling Norms

FSSAI’s labelling regulations require clear and accurate information on all pre-packaged confectionery products in India,
including candies, chocolates, and gums. Mandatory disclosures include the product name, ingredient list, nutritional
information, manufacturer details, FSSAI license number, net quantity, price, and allergen statements. The product name
must be prominently displayed on the Principal Display Panel.

Confectionery products must carry nutritional information per 100 g/ml and per serving, covering key nutrients such as
energy, sugars, fats, and sodium. Vegetarian or non-vegetarian symbols are mandatory, given the frequent use of milk-
based ingredients. Allergen and additive declarations, including INS numbers and required warning statements for
sweeteners such as aspartame, are compulsory where applicable.

                                   Table 10-11: FSSAI Regulation on Labelling Norms




                               Source: Food Safety and Standards (food product standards) regulations & Ken Research Analysis


                                                                            180
Regulatory Requirements for Exports

FSSAI regulations for export certification ensure that confectionery products exported from India comply with international
safety, quality, and labelling standards. Exporters are required to obtain relevant certifications such as Health Certificates,
Export/Import Permits, and Halal, Kosher, or Organic certifications, depending on the regulatory requirements of the
destination market. These certifications confirm compliance with product safety, origin, dietary standards, and
environmental norms applicable to confectionery products. Additional requirements may include FSMA compliance for
exports to the U.S. market, Certificates of Origin for tariff determination, and quality or sanitation certifications mandated
by importing countries. Proper export labelling for confectionery products covering ingredients, allergens, nutritional
information, and expiry dates is mandatory to ensure transparency and legal compliance in international markets.

Government Initiatives and Policy Support Pertaining to Confectionery Industry in India

The Indian government provides targeted policy support to the processed food and confectionery ecosystem, with a focus
on capacity expansion, MSME formalization, branding, and export competitiveness. Key schemes include:

    •    Pradhan Mantri Kisan SAMPADA Yojana (PMKSY), PMKSY directly supports the confectionery industry
         by strengthening back-end processing infrastructure critical for sugar-based and cocoa-based products,
         including mega food parks, common processing facilities, cold storage, and food safety testing labs.
          ✓ Access to plug-and-play infrastructure lowers capex barriers for confectionery manufacturers, especially
              MSMEs producing chocolates, sugar confectionery, bakery-linked sweets, and value-added jaggery products.
          ✓ The scheme’s scale (INR 10.6 thousand crore outlay) and approved projects (41 Mega Food Parks, 400+ cold
              chains) indirectly support confectionery clustering and contract

    •    PM Formalization of Micro Food Processing Enterprises (PMFME): It plays a foundational role in expanding
         the unorganised and regional confectionery segment, particularly traditional sweets, candies, toffees, jaggery-
         based confectionery, and bakery-linked products.

                                                                          181
         ✓    Through the One District One Product (ODOP) approach, several districts promote local sweet specialities
              (e.g., chikki, peda, laddu, jaggery confections), aiding branding, packaging upgrades, and market access.
         ✓    The scheme improves access to formal credit, food safety compliance (FSSAI), and modern packaging

    •    Make in India & FDI Policy Support: The liberalised FDI regime (100% FDI under automatic route in food
         processing) has directly benefited chocolate and confectionery multinationals operating manufacturing units in
         India.
          ✓ Enables global confectionery players to localise production, develop India-specific SKUs, and integrate India
              into global supply chains.
          ✓ Encourages technology transfer, modern processing, and quality benchmarking for domestic manufacturers.

    •    FSSAI Regulations & Product Standards: FSSAI standards for chocolates, sugar confectionery, cocoa products,
         fortification, and labelling provide regulatory clarity and consumer trust, which are essential for brand-led
         growth.
          ✓ Clear norms on cocoa solids, sweeteners, additives, and fortification enable innovation in healthier
               alternatives, functional, and child-focused confectionery.
          ✓ Strengthened food safety compliance improves acceptance in modern trade and exports.

    •    MSME & Credit-Linked Support: Confectionery manufacturing particularly at small and mid-scale is capital-
         intensive due to moulding lines, cooling tunnels, and packaging automation.
          ✓ Credit guarantee and interest subvention schemes improve access to finance for MSME confectionery units
              expanding capacity or upgrading technology.

Competition Landscape – India’s Confectionery Market

Major Confectionery Suppliers in the Industry

The Confectionery market is fragmented with ~20 large players such as Mondelez International, Hershey, Perfetti Van
Melle, Nestlé, Mars, Ferrero, and Amul, dominating the market with established brands and pan-India reach. Additionally,
there are 30+ agile SMEs, including Shellz India Limited, Prayagh Consumer, Kayeempe Foods, and Annapurna Swadisht
Ltd., which are carving out niche positions by focusing on affordable price points, localized flavors, and festival-driven
demand without relying on OEMs or co-manufacturers.

Distribution of confectionery is increasingly enabled by B2B Kirana aggregators like Jumbotail, ShopKirana, and Udaan,
which facilitate delivery and inventory management for Kirana stores. On the B2B retail side, modern trade players such
as D-Mart, Reliance Retail, and Spencer’s are key volume drivers.

Regulation of confectionery production is managed by agencies like Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI),
Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), and the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), which govern safety, standards,
and trade compliance.

Key Factors Shaping Competition

Competition in India’s confectionery market is shaped by brand equity, pricing flexibility, distribution reach, and innovation
agility. With the market expanding across both premium and mass segments, players must balance affordability with
differentiation while maintaining high product visibility and supply consistency.

                    Figure 0-37: Factors Shaping Competition in the India Confectionery Market




                                                             182
                                                     Source: Ken Research Analysis


Together, these dynamics establish a high entry and performance barrier, favouring companies that demonstrate
strong consumer trust, rapid innovation, and advanced distribution capabilities. Competitive intensity in the market
will increasingly hinge not only on pricing power but also on the strategic integration of data-driven marketing,
supply chain optimization, and localized product strategies to drive sustainable and scalable growth.

Company Profiling

Shellz India Limited

Shellz India Limited, based in Delhi and established in 2012, is a confectionery manufacturer in North India, positioned
in the INR 1–INR 10 value segment. The company operates across two core brand verticals namely, Hugs, and Tosca
covering Baked Treats, Choco Delights, Jellies, Panned and Sugar Candies and Food and Bakery Ingredients. Its business
model is anchored in a distributor-driven general-trade network, reaching neighboring states and institutional buyers. The
company’s focus is on affordable and innovative confectionery formats.

Prayagh Consumer Care Pvt. Ltd.

Prayagh Consumer Care Pvt. Ltd., based in Hyderabad, Telangana, is a sugar-confectionery manufacturer with three
Telangana plants and a portfolio spanning candies, toffees, éclairs, lollipops, jellies and chocolates under Cintu, Lavian and
Lavian Exotique. Formed via the 2023 NCLT-approved demerger of Prayagh Nutri Products’ confectionery division, it
now services almost 500,000 retail outlets and 10,000 wholesalers across India and exports to Latin America, Central
America and Africa.

Annapurna Swadisht Ltd.

Annapurna Swadisht Ltd., which acquired Indore-based Madhur Confectioners Pvt. Ltd. (MCPL) is based in
Kolkata, West Bengal, is a packaged foods and confectionery company. Through MCPL, it adds a portfolio of candies,
lollipops, premium moulded chocolates and cream-filled wafers and integrates ~300 MCPL distributors into Annapurna’s
wider national network, enhancing its reach in value and impulse confectionery across northern and central India. The
company offers a broad portfolio across candies (Cofilo, Truelove, Mr. Yummy, Lacto), lollipops (Fan Pop, Chilli Pop,
Rainbow Pop, Yogito), premium molded chocolates under the Doyana brand, and cream-filled wafers such as Speed
Breaker and Crispy. It offers playful product formats, novelty-driven flavors and affordable price-point architecture and
has presence across northern and central India, especially within the children’s confectionery category.

Kayempee Foods Pvt Ltd

Kayempee Foods Pvt Ltd., based in Hyderabad and incorporated in 1989, is a diversified confectionery manufacturer
with a product portfolio covering moulded chocolates, biscuits and cookies, wafer rolls, center-filled candies and éclairs,

                                                                183
gummies. The company is engaged in white-label and custom manufacturing, partnering with FMCG clients to deliver
tailored product development, flavor customization and packaging solutions, while simultaneously scaling its own brands
such as Pepe, Ausome, Byond, and Marco across value and mid-premium segments.

Dolphin Foods India Limited

Dolphin Foods India Limited, based in Hyderabad and founded in 1984, is a confectionery and baked-snacks
manufacturer with presence across Eastern and Southern India as well as a growing export footprint. The company
offers hard-boiled candies, toffees, lollipops, jellies, wafers, cakes and chocolates under its flagship Oshon and Otter brands,
along with specialty products such as healthier alternatives and fruit-flavored candies, premium cake bars and choco-filled
wafers. Dolphin Foods India Limited offers affordable, mass-market products with diverse flavor formats, supported by a
large assortment of SKUs including Cake Bar, Waffer Town, Coffista Candy, Mitha Paan, Magic Pop Lollipop, Assorted
Lollipops, Choc 7 Heartz, Wonderz Original, Eclairs Toffees and Peanut Rich.

Overview

We are engaged in the manufacturing and marketing of confectionery products in India, with a diversified product portfolio
comprising over 300+ SKUs across multiple categories, including choco delights, jellies, baked treats and other
confectionery formats. We also manufacture and supply food and bakery ingredients. We focus on developing
confectionery products at accessible price points and distributing them across a wide geographic footprint, including urban
and semi-urban markets, as well as smaller towns and rural areas.

According to Ken Report, the Indian confectionery market size was INR 93.1 thousand crore in FY’25 and is projected to
grow to INR 125.8 thousand crore by FY’30, at a CAGR of 6.3%. The market has demonstrated robust growth, expanding
at a CAGR of 9.1% between FY’19 and FY’25, driven by rising consumer demand for affordable indulgences, increased
frequency of festive consumption, and deeper penetration of packaged chocolate and sugar confectionery across both urban
and rural markets. Confectionery items priced between INR 1–10 accounted for the highest purchase intent at 86%,
indicating their dominant role in daily consumption patterns. The Indian confectionery market has seen a significant
transformation, driven by the shift in tastes of urban and semi-urban consumers. Small-pack, low-cost options priced under


                                                            188
INR 10 have penetrated Tier 2/3 cities, making innovative flavors and textures more accessible. India’s economy
confectionery market was valued at INR 50.5 thousand crores in FY’25, reflecting the continued relevance among price-
sensitive consumers, particularly in Tier 2–3 cities and rural areas. India consumed 523.0 million kg of confectionery, with
a per capita consumption of 0.37 kg in FY’23, which reached 0.39 kg by FY’25, substantially lower than countries like
Germany (14.4), USA (9.1), and Japan (3.2). Despite the low per capita figure, India's absolute population base is driving
total consumption reaching 576 million kg in FY’25, positioning it as a high-volume yet under-penetrated market. India’s
low per capita base presents significant room for expansion, with consumption projected to rise to 0.5 kg by FY’30E,
growing at a CAGR of ~4.6%. This growth is being driven by urbanization, rising incomes, a young population, and
increasing access to affordable SKUs.

We market our consumer products under two brands, “Hugs” and “Tosca”. Under our flagship “Hugs” brand, we offer
products across four categories, including baked treats, choco delights, jellies, and panned and sugar confectionery. The
“Hugs” portfolio is largely positioned at mass-market price points, with a majority of products priced at ₹10 or below.
According to the Ken Report, 68% of non-adult consumers opt for confectionery, including chocolate, at price points of
₹10 or below. Confectionery products are typically impulse-driven purchases, and sales are influenced by product
availability and visibility at retail points. According to the Ken Report, 92% of grocery consumption in India continues to
occur through Kirana stores. As on March 31, 2026, our products are distributed through a network of over 300 super
stockists and are available across kirana outlets in around 24 states in India. Our distribution model is focused on driving
volumes through repeat purchase-driven SKUs and wide retail penetration.

Under our “Tosca” brand, we offer products with a relatively higher unit selling price, positioned towards mass-premium
segments. The brand is currently being developed with a focus on e-commerce and quick commerce channels. The “Tosca”
portfolio comprises products with differentiated formats and packaging targeted at urban consumers. We are also expanding
the “Tosca” portfolio to include products incorporating cereal-based ingredients, aligned with evolving consumer
preferences for differentiated snacking options. As part of this portfolio, we formulated “Tosca Oat Choco”, an oat and
cereal-based bar positioned as an alternative to traditional confectionery formats, containing approximately 33% less sugar
than certain leading chocolate bars, based on internal product comparisons.

In addition to marketing and sales of consumer products under our own brands, we also undertake private label
manufacturing for third-party customers. We also export our products to international markets, including countries in the
Middle East, South Asia and Europe. These channels complement our core consumer business and support diversification
across customers, product formats and routes to market.

production and packaging, supported by quality assurance systems aimed at maintaining consistency in product quality.

     Our Strengths

     We believe that the following competitive strengths have contributed to our business growth and will continue to drive our
     success.

     a) Ability to develop differentiated products across formats and price points

     We focus on developing differentiated confectionery products across formats, categories and price points, supported by our
     understanding of consumer preferences across target markets. Our product portfolio includes a range of formats such as
     baked treats, choco delights, jellies, panned and sugar candies, food and bakery ingredients enabling us to cater to varied
     consumption occasions and consumer segments.

     Our approach to product development includes the introduction of products with distinct formats and combinations, aimed
     at enhancing consumer engagement within the confectionery category. For instance, we have developed products such as
     “Dip Sticks”, which combines biscuit sticks with chocolate cream, and “Push Up”, a cone-based cream and biscuit snack
     format designed for on-the-go consumption. These products reflect our focus on developing formats beyond traditional
     confectionery offerings, supporting the expansion of our product portfolio across categories and formats.

     We also develop products across a range of price points, including mass-market offerings as well as relatively higher-priced
     products under our “Tosca” brand. This allows us to address both mass-market and emerging demand for differentiated and
     premiumised products. As part of this approach, we have introduced products such as “Tosca Oat Choco”, an oat and cereal-
     based product positioned as an alternative to traditional confectionery formats.

     Our product development efforts are supported by an in-house team of food and packaging technologists who work on new
     product development, formulation and packaging formats. This enables us to continuously introduce new products and
     variants across categories in line with evolving consumer preferences. We believe our ability to develop products across
     multiple formats, while addressing different price points and consumption occasions, supports the expansion of our
     portfolio and helps us remain relevant across changing market preferences.

     b) Our presence at mass-market price-points supported by a diversified product portfolio

     A significant portion of our product portfolio is positioned at mass-market price points, with a majority of our SKUs priced
     at ₹10 or below. This aligns with consumption patterns in the Indian confectionery market, where a large share of purchases
     is driven by affordability and frequent, impulse-led consumption.

     Our focus on these price points enables us to participate in the mass-market segment characterised by repeat purchases and
     wide consumer accessibility. Products at these price points are typically distributed across several retail outlets and are
     consumed across urban, semi-urban and rural markets. This price-point positioning also supports accessibility across a wide
     consumer base, including school-going children, young consumers and households seeking affordable packaged
     confectionery products.

     We offer products across multiple confectionery categories at these price points, rather than relying on a limited number of
     SKUs or a single product type. This enables us to participate across multiple consumption occasions and consumer
     preferences while retaining relevance in value-driven segments of the market. Our ability to offer products across different
     categories, pack sizes and formats supports repeat purchases and allows us to address differing regional and retail
     requirements.

Our model is structured to support product movement through established channel partners, with a focus on ensuring
product availability across key markets. By leveraging the distribution networks of our super stockists and distributors, we
are able to expand our reach efficiently across regions. This distribution structure is particularly relevant in confectionery
categories where product availability at the point of sale plays an important role in supporting sales.

The use of super stockists also enables us to service multiple markets in a relatively scalable and cost-efficient manner,
while relying on local channel relationships and downstream market knowledge for product movement. This supports our
presence across kirana stores and other general trade outlets, which continue to be an important sales channel for the
category.

This approach enables us to optimise distribution costs while supporting consistent product availability across markets. It
also allows us to focus on product development and manufacturing, while utilising our distribution network for downstream
market coverage. We believe this model supports expansion of our geographic reach while remaining aligned with the
requirements of a multi-SKU confectionery portfolio.

d) Integrated in-house manufacturing capabilities with focus on scalability and process control

We manufacture our consumer products in-house at our production facilities, which enables us to maintain control over
product quality, manufacturing processes and production timelines. In-house manufacturing allows us to manage multiple
stages of the production process, including formulation, processing and packaging, and supports consistency across product
batches.

Our operations are supported by machinery sourced from multiple countries along with ancillary equipment from domestic
suppliers. This enables us to support production across a wide range of product categories and formats, including products
with varied ingredient compositions, textures and packaging requirements. The ability to manufacture diverse products in-
house also supports coordination between product development and production functions.

Our manufacturing infrastructure is designed to support production across a diverse portfolio of product categories and
formats, with defined processes across procurement, production and packaging. This allows us to respond to demand
requirements, manage production planning across product categories and support the introduction of new products and
formats as part of our product development efforts. It also enables us to manage products with differing production
requirements, including fat-based, milk-based, cocoa-based, water-based, and sugar-based confectionery formats, within
our overall manufacturing system.

We have an operational facility at Sonipat, Haryana, which is currently being utilised for manufacturing of packaging
materials used for captive consumption and warehousing. We are in the process of consolidating our existing operations
into this facility, along with undertaking expansion of production capacity. This consolidation is expected to support
improved integration of manufacturing and warehousing functions and streamline production and logistics operations over
time. As our operations expand, this facility is expected to support future growth across our existing and newly introduced
product categories.

Our manufacturing model also enables us to align production with the requirements of a multi-category portfolio, enabling
consistent supply across markets and facilitating efficient execution of our distribution model. We believe our in-house
manufacturing capabilities are an important enabler of both scale and product complexity across the business.

Our in-house product development capability supports coordination between product development and manufacturing

Our Strategies

We intend to strengthen our position and also growing our business at scale by implementing the following strategies:

a) Expand product portfolio to enhance product mix and improve margin profile

We intend to expand our product portfolio beyond our existing confectionery offerings into adjacent snacking categories
and differentiated product formats. This includes the introduction of products such as biscuits, premium biscuit variants,
cereal-based snacks and other packaged food products, along with continued development of confectionery products across
formats.

Our approach to product development focuses on expanding participation across multiple consumption occasions and
consumer segments by offering products across a range of formats, textures and price points. We intend to introduce
products that combine differentiated formats with accessible pricing, while also developing products positioned at relatively
higher price points under appropriate brand segments.

As part of our portfolio expansion, we also intend to develop products with improved contribution profiles through better
product mix and formulation choices. This includes evaluating products that are less dependent on input materials with
relatively higher price volatility, such as cocoa-based inputs, where commercially viable. We also intend to explore
ingredient compositions involving cereals, milk-based formulations and alternative blends, which may support more stable
cost structures across certain product categories.

In addition, we intend to expand our presence in products aligned with evolving consumer preferences, including products
positioned with relatively lower sugar content, reduced fat composition or alternative ingredient profiles, subject to

                                                            197
regulatory requirements and commercial feasibility. These products may be positioned within differentiated or higher-value
segments and are expected to complement our existing portfolio across categories.

Our product development efforts are supported by in-house capabilities across formulation, product trials and packaging
development, enabling us to evaluate new product concepts in a structured manner prior to scale-up. We aim to introduce
new products and variants on a continuous basis, while also optimising existing products based on market response and
operational considerations.

Through expansion across categories, formats and product profiles, we aim to build a diversified product portfolio that
supports participation across multiple consumption occasions, improves product mix and enhances our ability to respond
to evolving consumer demand.

b) Scale manufacturing capabilities and improve operational efficiency through our Sonipat facility

We have established an operational manufacturing facility at Sonipat, Haryana, which forms a key part of our strategy to
consolidate and expand our production capabilities. We are in the process of progressively integrating our existing
operations into this facility.

The Sonipat facility is designed to support higher production capacity and improved workflow efficiency through better
integration of manufacturing functions. Compared to our existing facilities, the Sonipat facility provides improved layout
planning, enabling more efficient material movement, reduced handling and better utilisation of available space.

We intend to enhance production efficiency at the Sonipat facility through the gradual implementation of automation and
semi-automation across manufacturing and packaging processes, where feasible. This is expected to support more
consistent output, optimise labour deployment and reduce operational inefficiencies over time.

The consolidation of operations at Sonipat facility is also expected to enable improved utilisation of installed machinery
and equipment by allowing for more streamlined production planning and reduced fragmentation across facilities. The
facility provides the flexibility to scale production across multiple product categories and formats as our portfolio expands.

In addition, the Sonipat facility is expected to support our ability to cater to a wider range of customer requirements,
including institutional customers and export markets, which may require higher consistency in production, packaging and
documentation processes.

We also intend to align our manufacturing processes at Sonipat facility with applicable food safety and quality requirements
relevant for both domestic and international markets, subject to regulatory and customer-specific standards.

Through the consolidation and expansion of operations at the Sonipat facility, we aim to improve operational efficiency,
support higher production volumes and strengthen our manufacturing capabilities as our business scales.

c) Build and scale the “Tosca” brand in higher-value product segments to enhance brand presence and improve
   product mix and margin profile

We intend to build and scale our “Tosca” brand as a platform for expanding our presence in relatively higher-value product
segments within confectionery and adjacent snacking categories. The “Tosca” brand is positioned to cater to distinct product
formats, ingredient combinations and packaging approaches, enabling us to participate in segments beyond our core value-
oriented offerings under the “Hugs” brand.

Under “Tosca”, we intend to develop and expand products across categories such as chocolate-based products, cereal-based
snacks, biscuit-based formats and other snack offerings. These products are expected to be positioned at relatively higher
price points and may incorporate varied textures, flavours and ingredient compositions.

We also intend to align the “Tosca” portfolio with evolving consumer preferences, including products with relatively lower
sugar content, alternative ingredient compositions and varied formats, subject to regulatory requirements and commercial
feasibility. This approach enables us to participate in consumption trends within organised retail and digital-led channels.

We intend to increase the presence of the “Tosca” brand through product placement, packaging differentiation, channel-
specific availability and digital platforms, in line with the positioning of the brand. We aim to expand the availability of
Tosca products across channels such as modern trade, e-commerce and other organised retail formats where such products
are more relevant.



                                                             198
The “Tosca” brand is expected to contribute to improving overall product mix by increasing the share of products with
relatively higher unit realisations within our portfolio. In addition, structured brand positioning and channel-specific
presence are expected to support improved recognition of the brand over time.

Through the development and scaling of the Tosca brand, we aim to expand our presence in higher-value segments, improve
product mix and support margin profile over time.

d) Expand geographic presence and deepen market penetration of our “Hugs” brand across India to drive volume
   growth

We intend to expand the geographic presence of our “Hugs” brand across India by increasing penetration in underpenetrated
regions and strengthening our presence in existing markets. Our expansion is supported by a super stockist-led distribution
model, which enables us to access a wide network of distributors and retail outlets in an efficient manner.

This model allows us to scale distribution across geographies without a field-intensive sales structure at the retail level,
supporting relatively faster market entry and expansion. We intend to continue strengthening this network by onboarding
additional super stockists and enhancing engagement with existing partners.

In addition to expanding geographic reach, we focus on deepening our presence within existing markets by increasing
product availability and widening assortment across retail outlets. We aim to increase the number of our products available
per outlet, thereby improving visibility and supporting increased offtake across our product portfolio.

Our “Hugs” product portfolio is positioned at accessible price points, enabling participation across a broad consumer base.
The nature of our product categories supports repeat consumption, which, combined with improved availability and
assortment, is expected to contribute to volume growth.

We also intend to align our product mix with regional consumption preferences by prioritising relevant SKUs across
different geographies. This approach enables us to improve acceptance and strengthen our presence within diverse markets.
Through a combination of geographic expansion, deeper market penetration and portfolio-led distribution, we aim to
increase volumes across our core product categories and strengthen the presence of the “Hugs” brand across India.

e) Expand presence across export markets through a segmented and margin-conscious approach

We intend to expand our presence across export markets by adopting a segmented approach based on product positioning,
regulatory requirements and market dynamics. Our export strategy is focused on aligning product offerings with the specific
requirements of different geographies rather than adopting a uniform approach across markets.

We intend to prioritise expansion in markets that support relatively higher unit realisations and require compliance with
defined quality, documentation and certification standards. Our manufacturing facility at Sonipat is expected to support
such requirements through improved process control and alignment with applicable food safety and regulatory frameworks,
subject to customer and market-specific requirements.

In parallel, we may continue to participate in price-sensitive markets where product specifications and regulatory
requirements differ. Our approach in such markets is expected to remain selective and aligned with product suitability,
commercial viability and capacity utilisation considerations. Over time, we intend to increase the share of exports to markets
that support relatively higher unit realisations, subject to regulatory requirements and commercial feasibility.

We intend to tailor our product portfolio for export markets based on local preferences, pricing dynamics and channel
requirements. This may include supplying both branded and customer-specific products, depending on the nature of the
market and customer engagement.

Our export strategy is also supported by our experience in dealing with international customers and suppliers, enabling us
to adapt to varying market requirements across geographies.

Through a segmented and calibrated approach to exports, we aim to expand our international presence, improve product
mix and support capacity utilisation over time.

Our Sales Channels

We employ a multi-channel sales approach to maximize availability and convenience for our consumers. Our structured
approach covers:


                                                             199
Super Stockist Model: In this model, we sell our products to super stockists, who purchase in bulk. Super stockists further
supply to distributors, who then distribute goods to Wholesalers, Intermediaries and Kirana Stores. This structure allows
products to move through multiple layers of trade until they reach retail shops, where they are purchased by consumers.

Online Platforms: We also sell through online platforms, including Amazon, Flipkart, Meesho, Kirana Club and Swiggy
Instamart. Orders placed through these platforms are fulfilled either through supply to central warehouses or through
marketplace fulfilment services. This online presence enables access to customers purchasing packaged confectionery
through e-commerce and facilitates visibility in digital retail channels.

Export Markets: Our products are also supplied to export markets, where we sell to overseas buyers based on orders
received. Export transactions are undertaken in compliance with relevant import regulations, packaging norms and labelling
requirements applicable in the destination country.

Private Labelling: We undertake private label manufacturing, where we manufacture products for third-party brands based
on specifications provided by them. These arrangements allow us to utilise spare manufacturing capacity for the brands that
market the product under their own label.

Modern Trade: In the modern trade channel, we supply our products to organised cash-and-carry retail formats. These
outlets cater primarily to bulk buyers, including retail customers as well as general trade store owners. Our presence in such
formats enables product placement through standardised merchandising and facilitates access to customers purchasing in
bulk quantities. This channel includes cash-and-carry stores such as Walmart, Metro and Lots.

Our Manufacturing Facilities

We currently manufacture our products at our manufacturing facility located at Samaipur, Delhi, which supports production
across our four key product categories such as baked treats, choco delights, jellies and panned & sugar candies. In addition,
we manufacture and supply food and bakery ingredients. The facility comprises defined production areas along with storage
for raw materials, work-in-progress and finished goods, enabling integrated manufacturing operations across categories.

In line with our expansion plans, we are in the process of consolidating and scaling our manufacturing operations at our
facility located at Sonipat, Haryana. Upon consolidation and expansion, our total installed production capacity is expected
to increase from approximately 17,100 MTPA to approximately 34,500 MTPA. The Sonipat facility is being developed to
support higher production volumes, improved process integration and enhanced operational efficiency across product
categories.



                                                                                                 200
The facility is structured into multiple processing zones designed to support specialised manufacturing requirements. These
include dedicated zones for polymer processing, sugar and panned candies, cream-based snacks, jellies (wet processing),
chocolate and fat-based products, and baking operations. This zonal configuration enables effective segregation of
processes, improved quality control and flexibility in handling diverse product formats within a single manufacturing
location.

Our manufacturing infrastructure at Sonipat is being aligned with applicable food safety and quality requirements relevant
for domestic and international markets, subject to regulatory and customer-specific standards. The facility is also designed
to enable efficient material flow and to support the gradual integration of automation across selected processes.

The Sonipat facility is strategically located within an established food processing cluster and benefits from strong
connectivity to key logistics infrastructure. It is situated in close proximity to the National Highway, enabling efficient
movement of goods. The facility is also located near the Barhi Mega Food Park, providing access to shared infrastructure
such as testing laboratories and cold storage facilities, as required. In addition, the presence of the National Institute of
Food Technology Entrepreneurship and Management (NIFTEM) in Sonipat supports access to a specialised talent pool and
technical ecosystem.

The facility is located within close proximity to ICD Baxi, facilitating efficient handling of containerised cargo for both
export and import operations. This enables streamlined outbound logistics for international shipments as well as efficient
inbound movement of imported raw materials and specialised inputs, supporting improved supply chain reliability and cost
efficiency.

Overall, the consolidation of manufacturing operations at the Sonipat facility is expected to strengthen our production
capabilities, enhance operational efficiencies, and support our ability to scale across product categories while aligning with
evolving market and regulatory requirements.

Business Model: Detailed Flow of Process

The brief detailed process of four principal product categories is mentioned below:

Baked Treats




                                                                       Cone and Wafer                   Cone and Wafer
   Raw Material and                 Chocolate and Milk                Batter Preparation                 Manufacturing
  Ingredient Handling               Cream Preparation                (Specific to cone and            (Specific to cone and
                                                                       wafer products)                  wafer products)




      Final Quality
                                       Secondary &                                                        Plastic Cup
      Assurance &                                                     Filling and Sealing
                                     Tertiary Packing                                                    Manufacturing
    Product Release




1. Raw Material and Ingredient Handling:

The baked confectionery category primarily uses chocolate cream, milk cream, biscuits, wafers, cones and food-grade
plastic components. Key ingredients include sugar, vegetable fat, cocoa solids, milk solids, wheat flour, raising agents,
additives and salt. All raw materials are received at the manufacturing facility, inspected for quality and compliance with
internal specifications, and stored under defined conditions prior to use in production.

2. Chocolate and Milk Cream Preparation:



                                                             201
Chocolate, milk and various other flavoured creams are prepared using high-speed mixers, where sugar, vegetable fat,
cocoa or milk solids and additives are blended to form a uniform mixture. The blended mass is refined using a refining mill
under controlled temperature to reduce particle size and achieve the desired texture. The finished cream is transferred to
stainless steel holding tanks with controlled agitation to maintain uniformity until the filling stage.

3. Cone and Wafer Batter Preparation (Specific to cone and wafer products):

Batter for cones and wafers is prepared in dedicated chilled high-speed batter mixers. Ingredients are mixed to achieve a
smooth, lump-free batter with controlled viscosity. Ingredient dosing is automated to ensure consistency across batches.
The prepared batter is stored in intermediate tanks with continuous agitation to prevent settling before baking.

4. Cone and Wafer Manufacturing (Specific to cone and wafer products):

Prepared batter is deposited into automatic cone baking machines or wafer baking drums. For cones, batter is baked in
heated cone-shaped moulds and formed into finished cones. For wafers, batter is baked on drums to form wafer sheets,
which are subsequently rolled into cylindrical wafer rolls while still pliable. The baked cones and wafers are then cooled
and stabilised prior to the filling process. Moisture levels are controlled within defined tolerances to ensure consistency in
texture and crunch.

5. Plastic Cup Manufacturing:

Food-grade plastic cups used in certain baked confectionery products are manufactured in-house using thermoforming
machines. Thermoplastic sheets are extruded from polymer granules and then moulded using male and female dies under
controlled vacuum, temperature and pressure conditions to achieve uniform wall thickness. The formed cups are cooled,
trimmed and automatically ejected for subsequent filling operations.

6. Filling and Sealing:

Cups, cones and wafers are fed into automated filling lines through stacker and conveyor systems. Multi-nozzle
temperature-controlled depositors dispense chocolate or milk cream into each unit, ensuring consistent fill weight and
controlled usage of filling material. Cups are sealed using heat-sealing or foil-lidding systems. Blister packs are formed
using thermoformed cavities, filled with cream and sealed with aluminium foil or sealing film to provide product protection
and tamper evidence.

7. Secondary & Tertiary Packing:

After primary sealing, products are transferred to secondary packaging tables, where they are packed into boxes, jars or
pouches suitable for handling and storage. Secondary packs are then placed into tertiary cartons or crates. Finished cartons
are labelled, stacked and sealed.

8. Final Quality Assurance & Product Release:

Finished products, after packaging, are subject to final quality evaluation to ensure compliance with defined quality and
food safety standards. This includes inspection of product appearance, weight conformity, packaging integrity and labelling
accuracy, along with applicable sensory and stability parameters. This final quality check serves as a control point prior to
storage and dispatch, ensuring that products delivered to the market meet internal specifications and applicable regulatory
requirements.

Choco Delights




                                                             202
     Raw Material

       Control

1. Raw Material Procurement and Control:

The chocolate manufacturing process begins with procurement of key raw materials including sugar, edible vegetable fat,
cocoa solids, milk solids, additives and salt. All incoming raw materials are received at the manufacturing facility and
subjected to defined quality checks. Materials are inspected for conformity with internal specifications and applicable food
safety regulations before being approved for use in production. Approved raw materials are stored under prescribed
conditions to maintain quality and stability.

2. Weighing, Mixing and Preparation:

Approved raw materials are weighed in accordance with approved formulations. The ingredients are then transferred to
mixing units where sugar, cocoa solids, vegetable fat, milk solids, additives, and salt are blended to form a homogeneous
chocolate mass. The mixing process is carried out under controlled conditions to ensure uniform distribution of ingredients.

3. Refining and Grinding:

The mixed chocolate mass undergoes refining and grinding under controlled temperature to reduce particle size, typically
to a fine range of approximately 20–22 microns. This step is critical to achieve the required texture and mouthfeel. Refining
equipment ensures consistency in particle size and uniformity across production batches.

4. Chocolate Depositing:

The prepared liquid chocolate is deposited into moulds using depositor machines that ensure controlled filling, uniform
weight, and consistent shape, enabling the production of both solid chocolates and centre-filled variants depending on
product requirements. The filled moulds are then passed through temperature-controlled cooling tunnels, where controlled
cooling enables proper crystallization of the chocolate, ensuring structural stability, smooth surface finish, and ease of
demoulding. Once the chocolate has fully set, the finished pieces are released from the moulds using demoulding systems
designed to prevent breakage or surface damage to the chocolates. This process is carried out in air-conditioned processing
areas to maintain controlled temperature and humidity conditions, ensuring product stability, consistency and quality.

5. Primary Packing:

Finished chocolates are transferred to primary packaging lines where they are packed according to the product format. Flow
wrap packaging is used for bars and individual units, foil wrap packaging is used for products requiring enhanced protection,
fold wrap packaging is used for select product presentations, and twist wrap packaging is used for select truffles. The
packaging materials are carefully selected to protect the products from moisture, air, and contamination, thereby helping
maintain product quality, freshness, and shelf life during storage and distribution.

6. Secondary and Tertiary Packing:

Primary-packed chocolates are grouped into boxes, pouches, or trays as part of secondary packaging. These units are then
placed into outer cartons or crates during tertiary packaging. Cartons are labelled, sealed, and prepared for storage and
dispatch.



                                                            203
7. Final Quality Assurance & Product Release:

Finished products, after packaging, are subject to final quality evaluation to ensure compliance with defined quality and
food safety standards. This includes inspection of product appearance, weight conformity, packaging integrity and labelling
accuracy, along with applicable sensory and stability parameters. This final quality check serves as a control point prior to
storage and dispatch, ensuring that products delivered to the market meet internal specifications and applicable regulatory
requirements.

Jellies


     Raw Material                                                                                      Controlled Stirring
                                       Mixing and                    Cooking and Gelling
   Procurement and                                                                                       and Process
                                     Homogenization                        Process
       Handling                                                                                           Monitoring




      Final Quality                                                                                     Manufacturing of
                                      Secondary and                  Filling, Sealing and
